newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia Aborigines firm on land rights.
newsitem.headline: Australia Aborigines firm on land rights.

text.p: Australian Aboriginal leaders said on Friday they remained firm on their demand to share land rights with farmers as the government seeks to resolve a row that farmers and miners say is damaging their industry.
Aboriginal leaders arriving at parliament house for talks with Prime Minister John Howard, said they were prepared to look at options as long as their rights were not abolished.
"We're very firm on our co-existence approach and rights of indigenous people," Gatjil Djerrkura, head of the peak Aborignal group, told reporters before the meeting.

Aboriginal negotiators said they are prepared to compromise to share rights to land, known as co-existence, and guarantee farmers' rights won't be eroded. But they insist any deal must not include extinguishment of their rights.
"Those options certainly will be considered in the light of that our rights are not extinguished," said Djerrkura, head of the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission (ATSIC).

The government is seeking to sort out confusion over land rights after a High Court ruling in December, known as the Wik case, that long-term pastoral leases did not automatically wipe out Aboriginal rights to land.
But the court did not spell out what rights Aborigines have.

Farmers say they cannot make business decisions until the government clarifies the issue with legislation. Some miners also operate on pastoral leases and the confusion has halted government processing of some exploration applications.
Farm lobby groups, backed by some key figures in the National Party, the junior partner in the coalition government, are demanding Howard legislate to completely quash Aboriginal land rights.
